```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lessR)
library(readxl)
library(BSDA)
read_excel("~/Downloads/butterflies_pesticides.xlsx")
butterflies_pesticide <-read_excel("~/Downloads/butterflies_pesticides.xlsx")
bp <- butterflies_pesticide
head(bp)
getwd()
system("git rev-parse --show-toplevel")
file.exists(".git")
list.files("butterflies_pesticides.xlsx", all.files = TRUE)
```
## Q1. Normality test 

```{r}
#Independent t-test
shapiro.test(bp$`Wing Length`)
```

## Q2. Equality of variances test

```{r}
head(bp)
var.test(`Wing Length`~ Group, data=bp)
```
## Q3. Statistical test

```{r}
#Welch's t-test
t.test(`Wing Length`~ Group, data=bp,
            alternative=c("two.sided"),
            var.equal=FALSE,
            )
```

## Q4. ggplot 

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(bp, aes(x=Group, y=`Wing Length`))+
  geom_boxplot()
```

## Q5. Summary  

```{r}
#I tested the effect of pesticide exposure on wing length in butterflies by comparing a group of pesticide-treated butterflies with an untreated control group (n = 80). Both groups were not departing from normality (Shapiro-Wilk, p > 0.05) but their variance was not equal (F-test p = 0.0055; Levine’s p = 0.0027) therefore I performed a Welch’s t-test. Wing length was significantly different among groups (t = 3.98, df = 66.03, p = 0.00017), with control butterflies having longer wings (632.18 ± 32.91 SD) than pesticide treated butterflies (593.49 ± 51.86 SD). This is a difference of ~ 38.7 units (95% CI: ~ 19 to 58) or a ~ 6% decrease in wing length. The effect size was considerable (Cohen's d = 0.89), indicating not only a statistically significant difference, but also one that is probably biologically important. Given the close relationship between wing size and flight ability, a loss of this magnitude could influence dispersal, feeding and mate-finding, suggesting that exposure to pesticides may have implications for the fitness of these butterfly populations in their environments.
```
